idiom_name: Slick DatabaseConfig.forConfig[JdbcProfile] + DAO class parameterized by the profile
implementation_notes: Slick documents this as the multi-database solution: DatabaseConfig.forConfig[JdbcProfile]("mydb") reads the profile (driver and dialect) plus connection settings from application.conf, and a DAO class parameterized by that profile (class DAO(val profile: JdbcProfile) { import profile.api._ }) stays store-agnostic while the profile supplies the dialect. The library owns the store-selection half - another backend is a configuration change plus a matching JDBC driver on the classpath - and the DAO classes remain hand-written. The classic abstract factory only appears when databases must be abstracted over in code rather than configuration.
pitfalls: Mixing two profiles breaks at compile time because the api imports are path-dependent; do not let two DatabaseConfig profiles meet in one DAO or shared query helper.
Blocking JDBC work still runs on Slick's AsyncExecutor thread pool; size that pool deliberately or DAO calls starve each other.
Config-driven selection hides typos in application.conf until DatabaseConfig is loaded; validate the store key and database at startup.

variants.name: Trait + companion-object factory
variants.idiom_name: trait UserDao + object UserDao { def apply(backend, xa): UserDao }
variants.implementation_notes: The container-free Scala form: a trait per DAO, one implementation per store, and a companion object whose apply or forBackend method returns the implementation for the configured backend - pattern matching on a sealed Backend ADT makes the selection total and exhaustive. This is the hand-written equivalent of the factory and the right one when no Slick-style profile abstraction is in use; a doobie Transactor per store works the same way, and the ADT pattern keeps store knowledge in one match.
pitfalls: A sealed ADT gives exhaustive matching, but repeating the match outside the companion object turns adding a store into a compile error across the codebase; centralise the one match.
Implicit or lazily initialised DAOs (implicit val, object initialisation) can capture a Transactor before it is configured; build DAOs explicitly at the composition root.
